surface_case: Stone restorer Marget Halloway accepts a routine three-week commission to assess and remove moss from a sunken moorland graveyard abandoned for forty years. The moss regrows overnight, localized cold spreads through the stones toward her, and her gloved employer, Arthur Penhaligon, repeatedly accelerates and obstructs the work while refusing to disclose his purpose.
true_case: The moss is a parasitic fungal network digesting the souls beneath the gravestones. Four years earlier, Marget's mentor and surrogate father, Oswin Kerrow, entered the barrow and made his own consciousness the network's central anchor so it would consume him instead of the other dead. Arthur Penhaligon is accelerating the decay to harvest what the network extracts for his own longevity. Marget can reconstruct the truth only by reading the stones through bare touch, permanently killing the nerves in her hands with every contact. To destroy the network and free Oswin, she must violate her defining principle by using an iron mallet to shatter the memorial stone that holds him, losing forever both the carved memory she swore to preserve and her ability to read stone.
core_question: What is eating the graves, and why does the raven never leave the fractured central stone?
emotional_question: Can Marget destroy the carved stone that preserves Oswin's last trace, freeing the man she loves as a father, when doing so violates the principle by which he taught her to live and costs her the only language in which she has ever understood the dead?
book1_promise: Across twelve slow, atmospheric chapters locked to Marget's third-limited perspective, each physical reading of the graveyard will yield another measurable piece of the mystery while advancing the numbness in her hands. Concrete discoveries will arrive every two to three chapters through cold patterns, material evidence, mapped measurements, and Oswin's non-explanatory field data. No dead person will speak or convey language, and no living character or document will explain the solution. The accumulating evidence will resolve into one answer in chapter 10, forcing Marget to choose between preserving Oswin's stone and ending his prolonged consumption.
book2_hook: No external sequel threat is introduced. The ending leaves an emotional and existential afterimage rather than an open case: Marget survives with permanently insensate hands, unable to read the history held in stone and unable ever to know whether Oswin wanted the release she gave him.
book1_ending_type: Closed tragic victory with irreversible personal sacrifice
reader_payoff_book1: Marget independently proves that the graveyard's cold spots form a root-like fungal network centered not merely on a location but on Oswin himself. She confronts Arthur's active attempt to preserve the harvest, takes up the iron mallet with hands already nearly numb, and shatters the central memorial stone. The fungal network dies, the other graves are released from its consumption, and Oswin's remaining presence vanishes with the last cold she will ever feel. The raven does not flee; once the stone is broken, it simply has nowhere to perch. Marget walks away across ground she can no longer read, having saved the dead and freed her mentor by destroying the memory she had sworn to preserve.
